justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with a modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 44.1 is anchored heavily to the most recent observed price or level, assuming mean-reverting dynamics dominate over such a short window with minimal new information arriving. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 44.25, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption — perhaps based on recent momentum or a slight bullish bias in underlying fundamentals. By the one-month horizon, the estimate rises to 44.5, continuing that gradual drift while also incorporating the possibility that any prevailing trend has more time to express itself. In all three cases, the point estimates are close together, suggesting I viewed the asset or variable as fundamentally range-bound with no strong directional catalyst expected.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% confidence interval spans roughly 1.75 units, meaning I had reasonably high conviction that short-term fluctuations would be contained — likely because intraday or overnight volatility tends to be relatively predictable. By one week, the interval widens to 3.5 units, capturing the possibility of a meaningful news event, sentiment shift, or macro data release disrupting the near-term equilibrium. At one month, the interval stretches to 7 units, acknowledging that over a 30-day window, central bank decisions, earnings reports, geopolitical developments, or liquidity shifts could all materially alter the trajectory.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected macro catalyst — such as a surprise rate cut, a major positive earnings announcement, or a sudden surge in risk appetite — could push the level well above 48. On the downside, a risk-off episode triggered by geopolitical escalation, a financial stress event, or a significant miss in key economic data could drive the level below 41. These tail scenarios were deliberately excluded from the central 90% range because I judged them unlikely but not impossible — they represent the roughly 10% of outcomes I did not capture.

It is also worth noting that model uncertainty itself is a source of risk that is difficult to fully quantify. My estimates assume the recent statistical regime persists, but structural breaks — a sudden change in volatility, a liquidity crisis, or a policy regime shift — could invalidate the distributional assumptions underlying these intervals entirely. In such cases, realized outcomes could fall well outside any interval derived from historical patterns, and that residual model risk is something no confidence interval can fully encapsulate.
